zh.q: 六种金属在火焰里各有各的颜色，这点颜色凭什么能当「化验报告」？
zh.concl: 根据火焰呈现的特征颜色，可以判断试样所含的金属元素，这种定性分析操作叫焰色试验（教材原话）。
points: 一个站位回答一个问题：怎么烧、六种试样、为什么滤黄、什么仪器、为什么发光。
六支试样瓶并排，才看得出「换一种盐就换一种颜色」。
屏上的 589.2 nm 是光谱仪给出的数，不是眼睛给的——眼睛只能说「黄」。

zh.q: 同一根铂丝连烧两种试样，第二次为什么还会带出上一种的颜色？
zh.concl: 每换一种试样，先把铂丝用盐酸洗净、在外焰上灼烧到与原来的火焰颜色相同；否则残留的钠盐会把黄色带过来（教材原话）。
points: 洗净的作用是把上一种试样的残留「洗掉 + 烧掉」，火焰回到空白。
盐酸把残留的钠盐溶走，教材指定用盐酸而不是只用清水。
这是本课的错误操作示范：不洗 → 黄色冒出来 → 要能解释是残留钠盐的 589 nm 亮起来了。

zh.q: 钠的黄色，为什么在光谱仪里是两条紧挨着的线？
zh.concl: 钠的黄光是 589.0 与 589.6 两条线（钠双线）；仪器分不开时只能读出中点 589.2，不能当成精确到 0.1 nm 的单一波长。
points: 颜色是眼睛给的粗数据，谱线是仪器给的细数据。
两条线的间隔 0.6 nm 由元素定，能不能分开由仪器的半高宽定。
分不开时读数报中点 589.2，这是仪器精度决定的；写成 589.0 就是假精度。

zh.q: 钾的焰色到底是紫是黄，为什么必须透过蓝色钴玻璃看？
zh.concl: 钾的紫色要透过蓝色钴玻璃才看得清——钴玻璃滤去黄光，把 589 nm 的干扰压到紫线的 1/18（教材脚注原话）。
points: 钾不是「有时紫有时黄」，而是紫色一直被钠黄盖着，滤掉黄才显出来。
干扰来自碳酸钾里的微量钠盐（教材脚注），不是钾本身显黄。
钴玻璃只压黄光，不改变钾的谱线位置（404.4 nm 不变）——它解决「看得见」，不解决「测得准」。

zh.q: 三种金属放出的光不一样，是因为「能量不一样」吗？
zh.concl: 每条谱线对应一对能级之差，E = hc/λ；不同元素的原子能级结构不同，跃迁放出的光能量不同，所以焰色不同（这就是教材练习 12 的答案）。
points: 颜色不同，本质是放出的光子能量不同。
能量越大 → 波长越短（偏紫）；能量越小 → 波长越长（偏红）。
钾最强的两条线在 766.5 / 769.9 nm（近红外）看不见，你看到的紫色来自 404.4 nm 那条弱的——「最强」和「最显眼」不是一回事。

zh.q: 同一个元素，发出来的光和吸掉的光，位置为什么一样？
zh.concl: 同一对能级：电子上去要吸这么多能量、下来就放这么多，所以吸收线与发射线位置相同；据此用特征谱线鉴定元素（铯 1860 年、铷 1861 年、氦 1868 年都是这样发现的）。
points: 吸收光谱和发射光谱不是两种元素，是同一个元素的两张照片。
位置一样，是因为能级差一样：上去要吸这么多，下来就放这么多。
光谱分析比焰色准：焰色会被微量钠盐骗，谱线不会。

zh.q: 把六种金属挨个烧一遍，颜色与谱线能对上一张表吗？
zh.concl: 焰色是判断金属元素最快的定性办法（不需要仪器）；光谱仪给出精确的谱线与能量。两者是同一原理（电子跃迁）的两级精度。
points: 六种颜色与教材表一一对应：先说颜色名，再说波长。
绿、砖红、洋红是带状光谱（分子带）贡献的：读数写「带状光谱的中心（示意）」，不叫谱线。
焰色回答「哪种元素」，光谱回答「哪条谱线、多少能量」。

zh.q: 考核：按教材的做法验出一支含钾试样
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：钾盐 + 洗净的铂丝 + 蓝色钴玻璃 + 发射光谱，四件事同时成立，才看得见钾的紫色。
points: 钴玻璃管「看得见」：把 589 nm 的钠干扰压下去。
洗净管「测得准」：残留钠盐连钴玻璃都压不住（1.91）。
发射模式才是看焰色，吸收模式是另一件事。

en.q: Six metals each give their own color in a flame. Why can that color serve as a "lab report"?
en.concl: From the characteristic color of the flame you can tell which metal element a sample contains; this qualitative analysis is called a flame test (textbook wording).
points: Each station answers one question: how to burn, the six samples, why filter yellow, what instrument, why it emits light.
With six sample bottles side by side you can see "change the salt, change the color".
The 589.2 nm on screen comes from the spectrometer, not the eye; the eye can only say "yellow".

en.q: Burn two samples in a row on the same platinum wire. Why does the second still show the first one's color?
en.concl: Before each new sample, wash the platinum wire with hydrochloric acid and heat it in the outer flame until the flame matches its original color; otherwise leftover sodium salts carry the yellow over (textbook wording).
points: Cleaning "washes off + burns off" the previous sample's residue so the flame returns to blank.
Hydrochloric acid dissolves leftover sodium salts; the textbook specifies hydrochloric acid, not just water.
This is the lesson's wrong-procedure demo: don't clean → yellow appears → explain that leftover sodium salt's 589 nm line has lit up.

en.q: Why does sodium's yellow appear as two lines close together in the spectrometer?
en.concl: Sodium's yellow light is two lines, 589.0 and 589.6 (the sodium doublet); when the instrument can't separate them you can only read the midpoint 589.2, not a single wavelength accurate to 0.1 nm.
points: Color is coarse data from the eye; spectral lines are fine data from the instrument.
The 0.6 nm gap between the lines is set by the element; whether they separate is set by the instrument's line width (FWHM).
When they can't be separated, report the midpoint 589.2; that's the instrument's precision, and writing 589.0 is false precision.

en.q: Is potassium's flame purple or yellow, and why must you look through blue cobalt glass?
en.concl: Potassium's purple is only clear through blue cobalt glass: the glass filters out yellow, pushing the 589 nm interference down to 1/18 of the violet line (textbook footnote wording).
points: Potassium isn't "sometimes purple, sometimes yellow": its purple is always covered by sodium yellow and only shows once the yellow is filtered.
The interference comes from traces of sodium salt in the potassium carbonate (textbook footnote), not from potassium itself being yellow.
Cobalt glass only suppresses yellow light and doesn't move potassium's line (404.4 nm stays): it makes it "visible", not "measured accurately".

en.q: The three metals give different light. Is that because of "different energy"?
en.concl: Each spectral line corresponds to the gap between a pair of energy levels, E = hc/λ; different elements have different atomic energy levels, so their transitions emit light of different energy and their flame colors differ (this is the answer to textbook exercise 12).
points: Different colors fundamentally mean different photon energies.
Higher energy → shorter wavelength (toward violet); lower energy → longer wavelength (toward red).
Potassium's two strongest lines are at 766.5 / 769.9 nm (near-infrared) and invisible; the purple you see comes from the weak 404.4 nm line. "Strongest" and "most visible" aren't the same.

en.q: For the same element, why are the light it emits and the light it absorbs at the same positions?
en.concl: Same pair of levels: an electron absorbs exactly as much energy going up as it releases coming down, so absorption and emission lines are at the same positions; characteristic lines identify elements (caesium in 1860, rubidium in 1861 and helium in 1868 were all discovered this way).
points: Absorption and emission spectra aren't two elements; they're two pictures of the same element.
The positions match because the energy gap is the same: going up absorbs exactly as much as coming down releases.
Spectral analysis is more accurate than flame color: flame color can be fooled by traces of sodium salts, spectral lines can't.

en.q: Burn the six metals one by one. Do the colors and lines match a single table?
en.concl: Flame color is the fastest qualitative way to identify a metal (no instrument needed); a spectrometer gives precise lines and energies. They are two levels of precision of the same principle (electron transitions).
points: The six colors match the textbook table one to one: name the color first, then the wavelength.
Green, brick red and magenta come from band spectra (molecular bands): the reading says "band center (illustrative)", not a spectral line.
Flame color answers "which element"; the spectrum answers "which line, how much energy".

en.q: Assessment: detect a potassium-containing sample using the textbook method
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: potassium salt + clean wire + blue cobalt glass + emission spectrum must all hold at once to see potassium's purple.
points: Cobalt glass handles "visible": it suppresses the 589 nm sodium interference.
Cleaning handles "accurate": leftover sodium salt is too much even for cobalt glass (1.91).
Emission mode is for viewing flame color; absorption mode is a different thing.
